name: Palácio da Bolsa (Stock Exchange Palace)
short: The Neoclassical palace of Porto's Commercial Association, begun in 1842 on the site of a burnt monastery and famous for its Alhambra-inspired Arab Room.
long: The Stock Exchange Palace, or Palace of the Porto Commercial Association, was begun in October 1842 after the old exchange closed and merchants were left to do business in the open street. It rose on the site of the São Francisco monastery, destroyed by fire in 1833. Over the decades several architects worked on it, blending Neoclassical, Tuscan and English Neo-Palladian motifs. Its highlight is the Arab Room (1862–1880), covered in gilded arabesques, where Porto receives visiting heads of state. The palace remains the headquarters of the Commercial Association and is open for guided tours.
history:
Construction of the Stock Exchange Palace began in October 1842. It was prompted by the closure of the city's old trading house (Casa da Bolsa do Comércio), which forced Porto's merchants to discuss deals outdoors on Rua dos Ingleses. The site had previously held the São Francisco monastery, burnt down in 1833 during the siege of Porto.

Several architects worked on the palace in succession: Joaquim da Costa Lima (1841–1860), Gustavo Adolfo Gonçalves de Sousa (1860–1879), Tomás Soller (1879–1883), José Macedo de Araújo Júnior (1883–1890), Joel da Silva Pereira (1894–1899) and José Marques da Silva (1900–1910). The first phase was largely ready by 1848, though the decoration continued for decades.

The best-known room is the Arab Room (Salão Árabe), created between 1862 and 1880 by Gonçalves e Sousa after the Alhambra in Granada. Its walls and ceiling are covered in gilded stucco with Arabic inscriptions. State receptions for visiting heads of state are held here.

The Nations' Courtyard (Pátio das Nações) is roofed in glass and decorated with the coats of arms of the countries Porto traded with; around it lie the Golden Room, the Assembly Rooms and the Portrait Room. The building serves as the headquarters of the Porto Commercial Association and as a venue for cultural, social and political events.

In 1982 the palace was declared a Portuguese national monument. In 2014 it drew more than 250,000 visitors, making it one of the city's most popular monuments.
facts: The first stone was laid in October 1842.
The Arab Room was created between 1862 and 1880 by Gonçalves e Sousa, inspired by the Alhambra.
It stands on the site of the São Francisco monastery, burnt in 1833.
Six architects worked on the project, including José Marques da Silva.
It has been a Portuguese national monument since 1982.
It is the headquarters of the Porto Commercial Association.
tip: The palace can only be seen on a guided tour, departing roughly every 30 minutes; tickets are sold at the door, so arrive at opening time in high season. It sits right beside the Church of São Francisco in Ribeira, so the two are easy to visit back to back. Photography is allowed without a tripod indoors; the most striking shots are the glass-roofed Nations' Courtyard and the Arab Room.
